query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reduce the stand-off distance during APS from 100 mm to approximately 80 mm to minimize in-flight oxidation and particle scatter, thereby increasing coating build-up and integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited with a current stand-off distance of around 100 mm, resulting in a 15–45 μm thick layer.
generation.intervention: Decrease the stand-off distance from 100 mm to approximately 80 mm while keeping all other spray parameters constant, with supervisory adjustments to traverse speed and gas flow as needed.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric plasma spraying under standard operating conditions with pre-treated substrates; service conditions involve high-temperature operation in thermal barrier coat systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A shorter stand-off distance reduces the flight time of particles, limiting exposure to ambient oxygen and reducing material scatter; the resulting higher particle kinetic energy improves splat formation and coating cohesion.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the distance, hot particles reach the substrate quicker, which limits oxidation and provides greater momentum for splat flattening. This promotes a thicker and more uniform deposit.
generation.predicted_outcome: The resultant bond coat will be thicker than the baseline with similar or diminished levels of oxidation, while maintaining robust adhesion and microstructural integrity.
generation.baseline: Deposition at a stand-off distance of 100 mm that produces a 15–45 μm coating with typical oxidation levels and splat morphology.
generation.boundary: Reducing the stand-off distance further than approximately 80 mm may risk substrate overheating, excessive kinetic impact causing splashing, or non-uniform deposition; thus, 80 mm is proposed as a safe lower limit.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal distance might vary with spray system configuration; experimental tuning is necessary to fully optimize the balance between reduced oxidation and avoiding substrate damage.

falsification_experiment.design: Execute APS depositions at stand-off distances of 100 mm (baseline), 90 mm, and 80 mm while maintaining constant other parameters. Evaluate coating thickness, uniformity, oxidation levels, and substrate thermal effects using SEM, XRD, and thermal imaging.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the stand-off distance to 80 mm does not lead to a statistically significant increase in coating thickness, or if substrate overheating, splashing, or increased oxidation occurs, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC. cited_evidence.kind: web:2.3. Atmospheric Plasma Spraying Coating of Samples
cited_evidence.text: Pre-heating of the processed HEA powder was carried out by placing it in the oven for 2 h at 25–150 °C, to remove any moisture present. The substrates were pre-heated with the flame of the spraying gun before the powder feed start. Plasma sprayed samples were manufactured by conventional Atmospheric Plasma Spraying system (Metco 9MC, Sulzer Metco Inc., Westbury, NY, USA) using a stand-off distance of 250 mm. Argon (Ar) gas was employed as the primary plasma operating gas and hydrogen (H2) was used as the secondary gas to escalate the whole plasma jet temperature. The feedstock ball milled powder was conveyed by a separate argon source and inoculated superficially into the spawned plasma jet at an angle of 90° concerning the anode axis. After that plasma torch assembly was mounted onto a robotic arm (YR-SK16-J00 Motoman, Yaskawa Electric Corp, Fukuoka, Japan) to navigate across the substrate holders for coating. All the parameters of the plasma spraying operation are enlisted in Table 1.

The roughness of the thermal sprayed coatings can be adjusted by optimizing the parameters while spraying that include stand-off distance, power, voltage, and feedstock morphology as reported by Anupam et al. []. Li, Zuhao, et al. reported that the roughness of the alloy improved after the heat treatment []. In the case of plasma-sprayed samples, the roughness values were found to be higher than that of annealed coatings. Different particles experience different heating temperatures during flight and projection towards substrate thus forming splats on the substrate surface upon complete or partial melting. These partially melted particles forming splats upon cooling give rise to higher values of roughness. While in the case of annealing treatment of coatings the roughness values were found to be lowered, this is consistent with the diffusion process as the temperature applied in annealing favored the alloy formation and grain refinement which resulted in a fine microstructure and lower roughness values.
